sections.h2: Where to record a deed in Tarrant County
sections.html:
Land records go to Records Intake in Room B20 of the historic Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. Land-related documents can be recorded only there, not at the sub-courthouses.

Filing works three ways: in person from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, by post with the original plus a check or money order made out to the Tarrant County Clerk, or through the county's eRecording process. Walk-in filers must show a driver's license or ID, while mailed documents do not need a copy of one.

Staff will not notarize, advise you on the law or fill in forms for you. Get the deed notarized ahead of time. Intake takes only originals or clerk-certified copies.

On most documents the first page costs $20 and every page after it $4. A notice of trustee sale runs $10. Printing on both sides of a sheet counts as two pages.

Tarrant County Clerk fees
ServiceFee
Recording, first page$20
Recording, each added page$4

Copy made in person or by mail, per page$1

Unofficial watermarked copy onlineFree

The counter takes cash, cards, checks and money orders, and cards add a small convenience fee. Some document types follow different fee rules, so confirm yours with the clerk.

The County Clerk Official Records Search is free to browse. Once you find a document, register for an account and download an unofficial watermarked copy at no charge. That is enough for your own research.

If a lender or title company wants a certified copy, you can buy one through the same system. Choose the certified-copy icon, pay the calculated fee, then pick up the file under Order History in your account. Certified copies are also sold in person at Room B30 of the courthouse, or by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope and the document number.

New filings do not appear instantly. Expect a recorded document to turn up on the search site 5 to 7 business days later. Intake scans and indexes it while you wait and hands you an instrument number, which is your proof of filing in the meantime. Title searches, lien searches and restriction reviews are not done by clerk staff. A title company handles them.

sections.h2: What the clerk will and will not record
sections.html:
Records Intake takes documents that the law allows to be recorded, chiefly those that concern land: deeds, deeds of trust, liens and releases, some land affidavits, and plats.

Four kinds of documents get turned away:

  • Documents with no statutory authority behind their filing.
  • Documents that are not regular on their face.
  • Documents not properly signed in front of an officer such as a notary.
  • Copies that are neither originals nor clerk-certified.

Wills get special treatment. Intake records only probated wills, and a person who wants a will kept at the courthouse can leave it with the Probate office in Room B90 for a $5 fee. A conveyance must be signed and acknowledged, or sworn before two witnesses, under Texas law before it is recorded. Common deed types include general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds.

sections.h2: Why recorded documents matter when you sell
sections.html:
Before closing, the buyer's title company reads every recorded document on your parcel, and anything left unreleased can hold up the sale. Common trouble spots are an old deed of trust never released, a lien, an affidavit that clouds title, and a missing deed on an inherited property.

A tax lien exists without any recording. It attaches every January 1, and clear title is impossible for a buyer until delinquent taxes are paid. Liens filed by the state comptroller are recorded with the county clerk, so you may see them in the clerk's records.

Once a lender begins foreclosure, a notice of trustee sale shows up in the clerk's records. Foreclosure sales in Texas are auctions, and for unpaid taxes a constable or an agent hired by the taxing unit runs the sale. Seeing that notice on your house still leaves choices: repay the debt, list the house, or accept a cash offer that closes ahead of the sale date.

sections.h2: Probate and the rest of the clerk's work
sections.html:
The county clerk serves as recorder, as clerk of the commissioners court, and as the office receiving probate filings like applications and small estate affidavits. In Tarrant County the real property side and the probate side sit in different rooms of the same courthouse, with probate in Room B90.

If the house came to you after someone died, the split affects your timing. Heirs may need probate papers filed before anyone can sign a deed, and those go through a different line than the deed. Plan a separate trip or mailing for each, and ask the title company what must be recorded first.

Title companies and escrow agents also have account options. An OPR Escrow Payments route exists for the Official Public Records, with 817-884-1062 for completing the process after an online payment, and a separate bulk data payment route at 817-884-1069. Most individual sellers never need either, but your title company might use the first.

Tarrant County offers a Property Fraud Alert sign-up, linked from its Real Estate Records page. Use that link to see how alerts work and what they cover.

A yearly check or two of your own name and address in the Official Records Search is a smart habit. Watch for any deed or lien you cannot explain, and if one appears, carry its instrument number to the clerk and to a title company.

Recording is public by design. That helps buyers and lenders trust the chain of title, but it also means anyone can see what was filed against your parcel, and a forged deed that gets recorded still has to be unwound through the courts.

sections.h2: Preparing your papers for a sale
sections.html:
Whether you plan to list or accept a cash offer, start by downloading your recorded deed from the Official Records Search and reading it. Check that every owner name is spelled correctly and that the legal description matches your tax bill. Errors found now are far cheaper to fix than errors found at the closing table.

  1. Search your name and address for any deed of trust and confirm it was released after payoff.
  2. Look for liens, judgments or affidavits filed against the parcel.
  3. If the house was inherited, confirm the probate papers and the deed into your name were filed.
  4. Order a certified copy of anything the title company asks for.
  5. Get the deed notarized before you go to Room B20, or mail it with the right fee.

A cash buyer still needs a title company to examine these records, but the lack of a lender's underwriting means fewer parties waiting on paperwork.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Tarrant County?
faqs.a: Most documents cost $20 for the first page and $4 for each added page. A document printed on both sides counts as two pages.

faqs.q: Where is the Tarrant County Clerk's records office?
faqs.a: Records Intake is in Room B20 of the Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. It is open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed by mail in Tarrant County?
faqs.a: Yes. Mail the original to Room B20 with a check or money order payable to the Tarrant County Clerk, and work out the fee from the page count. The deed must already be notarized.

faqs.q: Can I get a copy of my deed for free?
faqs.a: Yes, an unofficial watermarked copy downloads free from the Official Records Search after you register for an account. Certified copies cost $1 per page plus $5 for certification.

faqs.q: How long before a recorded deed shows online in Tarrant County?
faqs.a: Generally 5 to 7 business days after recording. Walk-in filers get an instrument number while they wait.
